title: Para que lo entiendas
blurbEn: A word that means everything and nothing, and the conjunction that always takes the subjunctive: para que.
body:
Le escribo a Pablo para que me explique una cosa.

En México dicen «ahorita» todo el tiempo y yo nunca sé qué significa.

—Depende —contesta—. Puede ser ahora mismo, dentro de diez minutos o nunca.

—¿Y cómo lo sabéis?

—Por el tono. Te lo digo para que no esperes sentada.

Le mando un mensaje a mi hermana para que se ría. Ella me manda otro para que yo me ría también, con una lista de palabras españolas que tampoco significan nada concreto: «luego», «un rato», «enseguida».

Me hace gracia que un país entero se ponga de acuerdo en ser impreciso.

Todos los idiomas tienen palabras así. Sirven para que la gente no tenga que comprometerse.

Es una forma de cortesía. Y también, a veces, una forma de escapar.
translationEn:
I write to Pablo so that he can explain something to me.

In Mexico they say "ahorita" all the time and I never know what it means.

"It depends," he replies. "It can be right now, in ten minutes, or never."

"And how do you know which?"

"From the tone. I'm telling you so you don't sit around waiting."

I send my sister a message to make her laugh. She sends me another to make me laugh too, with a list of Spanish words that don't mean anything specific either: "luego", "un rato", "enseguida".

It amuses me that a whole country has agreed to be imprecise.

Every language has words like this. They exist so that people don't have to commit themselves.

It's a form of politeness. And also, sometimes, a form of escape.

explique.note: 'para que' takes the subjunctive without exception — a purpose is by definition not yet achieved.

ría.note: Subjunctive of 'reír'. Note the accent: 'ría', not 'ria'.

ponga.note: 'ponerse de acuerdo' is to reach an agreement.

phrases.gloss: so that he explains to me
so you don't sit around waiting
